coherence.reasons: Both use a governing thought, four supporting claims and matching sections. Y's chain is tighter: demand is smaller than claimed, so timing favours mobile, so package in Pro, so plan and gates; each slide title supports its section claim. Y's one tension is that the 1.9x timing headline leaves out the $257K a quarter of Pro contribution it discloses on the same slide. X has more loose joints. Its first claim compares $8M of ARR with $0.8M of gross profit. Its packaging claim ('AI must sit inside a plan') is supported by a slide showing the win-back is small, which does not support it. Gate 1 falls back to the add-on in Q2, although X's own stress case says low uptake favours mobile first. X also asks for approval of the Q2 launch and the engineers before the Q1 test that is meant to decide it.

judgment.reasons: Both conclusions meet the key's criteria: X is R1 (launch in Pro with an allowance, accepting the mobile delay explicitly), and Y is R3 with the win-rate risk quantified ($160K a quarter plus $121K of AI churn) and a fallback to a Q2 launch. X weighs the alternatives more fully. It gives a base and a stress case, a break-even uptake of about 25% at which the order flips, an admission that Copilot first wins 'only narrowly', and four gates that each carry a threshold, a date and an action. It keeps the add-on as a tested fallback. Its weak point is counting shifted Pro ARR as NRR forgone, set against permanent churn. Y's point that Pro revenue is shifted, not lost, and that Pro lifts NRR only once, is sound. But its 1.9x headline excludes the Pro contribution it discloses; including it brings the two sides roughly level, so Y's call is as narrow as X's but presented as clear. Y's gates mostly lack an action if crossed, and its interim AI response is thin (a price test and keeping beta payers served) while Routewise sells AI for two to three more quarters.

evidence.reasons: Both get the required numbers right: $8.06M against $2.45M, inference of $32.4, $61.2 and $130.5 a month, about $0.6M of win-back, and $2.9M for Pro. Both flag the survey bias, the volunteer bias, the Routewise discount and the sales memo overreach, which each sizes at $1.9M or three times the whole drop. Y adds that the add-on margin is 58.9% for buyers and 12.4% for the top tenth, that loss notes cover all losses and not only Routewise, that a 90-day renewal window says little about annual churn, and a Pro contribution at mean usage of $1.03M. X adds that new-customer ARR does not count toward NRR, that the 2023 tier had no AI, and the full bridge from $8M to $0.8M. The difference is in inference quality. Y sets its allowance at 854 requests per seat, exactly the level where company margin hits 75%, leaving no buffer while noting heavy users move first. Its 1.9x headline also omits a cost it quantifies itself. X's allowance of 333 per seat is derived from a 75% margin on the Pro premium and tested at full use. X's flaw is equating delayed Pro uptake with lost NRR, which it partly offsets by calling the result narrow and the mobile figure a ceiling.

revision.reasons: Both revise the CPO's hypothesis as the evidence requires. Each rejects the $8M survey sizing in favour of the paywall rate and calls even that a ceiling, and each replaces the flat $149 add-on with Pro plus a usage allowance because heavy users select into it. X keeps the part the evidence supports, a Q2 launch, makes the mobile trade-off explicit and gates it, and holds the add-on as a tested fallback. Y revises further by delaying the launch to Q4, which the key allows when the mobile trade-off is argued explicitly; Y does argue it and sides with the Head of Customer Success on the evidence. The key says launching is supported and expects launch kept with packaging and sizing revised, which is closer to X; Y's further step rests on a timing ratio that is weaker than stated.

overall.reasons: Both are strong documents that avoid every trap and reach defensible conclusions with correct arithmetic. X serves the decision maker somewhat better. It shows how sensitive the recommendation is (the order flips below about 25% Pro uptake and the result is narrow). It pairs each gate with a threshold, a date and a concrete switch. Its allowance design leaves margin headroom. It runs a randomised test of both offers before launch. Y's storyline is cleaner and it has real insights: Pro revenue is shifted, not lost, and Pro lifts NRR only once. But its central timing claim of 1.9x overstates a comparison that its own disclosed Pro contribution brings close to parity, its allowance sits exactly at the margin floor, and its gates are mostly monitoring thresholds without actions. X's weaknesses are treating delayed Pro ARR as forgone NRR and committing the engineers before the test reads out; it is open about how close the call is.
